question: What is the main reason nurses perform a nutritional assessment on a patient?

options.A: To calculate the exact cost of the patient's hospital meals
options.B: To prescribe specific dietary supplements right away
options.C: To diagnose rare genetic disorders affecting metabolism
options.D: To check nutritional status and spot any shortages or excesses early

explanation: Spotting nutritional imbalances early helps you start the right care plan before things get worse. You've got this!

question: Can an overweight patient still suffer from poor nutrition? If so, why?

options.A: Yes, because body weight doesn't show the quality of micronutrients consumed
options.B: Yes, because overweight people cannot absorb proteins at all
options.C: No, because excess body fat stores all necessary vitamins forever
options.D: No, because larger people always have fast metabolisms

explanation: A person can eat plenty of calories and still lack essential vitamins and minerals. That's hidden malnutrition!

question: What is the main drawback of using a 24-hour dietary recall to check a patient's food intake?

options.A: It relies heavily on the patient's memory
options.C: It only measures water and ignores solid food
options.D: It takes over three hours to complete

explanation: Patients easily forget small snacks or misjudge portion sizes when trying to remember everything they ate yesterday.

question: A nurse asks an older patient how many times a week they eat fresh fruits and vegetables. What assessment tool is the nurse using?
explanation: Asking how often specific foods are eaten over a weekly or monthly span is a classic food frequency questionnaire.

question: If a hospitalized patient experiences sudden, rapid weight changes, what is the most likely cause?
explanation: Body fat and muscle don't pile on or waste away in just a few hours or days. Quick scale changes usually mean water weight!

question: Why is it so helpful to compare a patient's current weight to their usual baseline weight?

options.A: It proves the weighing scale is working properly
options.B: It helps spot meaningful weight gains or losses over time
options.C: It is the only legal requirement for ward admission charting
options.D: It completely replaces the need for a BMI calculation

explanation: Comparing against the patient's own baseline shows personal health trends that standard population charts might miss.

question: Which parts of the body usually show signs of nutritional shortages first?

options.A: Deep dense bones like the femur
options.B: Hard cartilage located in the joints
options.C: Tissues with rapid cell turnover like skin and hair
options.D: Large skeletal muscles in the thighs

explanation: Cells that divide quickly need a constant supply of nutrients, so they show outward signs of shortage first.

question: Which physical finding is a classic sign of severe protein deficiency?

options.D: Dry, brittle, and easily pluckable hair

explanation: Protein builds hair shafts. When protein is low, hair becomes weak, dry, and pulls out very easily.

question: Which physical check is a reliable sign of dehydration, especially in older adults?

options.A: Increased muscle tone in the upper arms
options.B: Dry mucous membranes inside the mouth
options.C: Cool skin temperature in the lower legs
options.D: Reduced skin turgor on the back of the hand

explanation: Skin turgor can be tricky in older adults due to aging skin, but checking inside the mouth for moisture is very reliable.

question: A patient has swollen ankles, bulging neck veins, and crackles in the lungs. What do these signs point to?
explanation: When water builds up in the tissues and lungs, you get swelling, bulging veins, and lung crackles. That's fluid overload!

question: Why do healthcare workers often check serum prealbumin instead of albumin to track recent nutritional changes?

options.A: It measures total body fat instead of protein
options.B: It has a shorter half-life and responds faster
options.C: It is much cheaper to run in any lab
options.D: It never changes during an infection

explanation: Prealbumin leaves the body quicker, meaning it shows recent nutrition improvements or drops much faster than albumin.

question: What is an important thing to remember when looking at a low serum albumin level in a sick patient?

options.A: Albumin also drops during inflammation, which can look like malnutrition
options.C: Albumin levels always spike right after a high-fat meal
options.D: Lab errors make albumin completely useless in hospitals

explanation: Infection and body stress trigger inflammation, which lowers albumin levels even if the patient's diet is fine. Keep this in mind during clinicals!

question: Which nursing goal for a malnourished patient is written clearly and measurably?

options.A: Patient will stop refusing meals when nurses enter
options.B: Patient will feel much better about hospital food soon
options.C: Patient will gain ten pounds of pure muscle by tomorrow morning
options.D: Patient will eat at least 75 percent of meals within 48 hours

explanation: Great nursing goals have a specific target (75%) and a clear timeframe (48 hours) so you can easily check your progress.

question: Which healthcare professional should you team up with when a patient has trouble chewing or swallowing?
explanation: Speech therapists are experts at assessing swallowing disorders and helping patients eat safely. Teamwork makes the dream work!
